title: Getting ready for the first day of preschool
summary: Small, simple steps that help a young child, and their parents, feel ready for a happy start at preschool.
coverAlt: Two children working together at a classroom table
intro: The first day of preschool is a big step for a little person, and often for their parents too. A few small routines in the weeks before can turn nervous excitement into a confident start.

sections.heading: Talk about it, cheerfully
sections.text: Mention preschool now and then in everyday chat: the friends your child will meet, the songs they will sing and the toys they will play with. Keep it light and positive, and answer questions simply and honestly.

sections.heading: Practise the new routine
sections.text:
A week or two before school starts, move bedtime and wake-up time to match the school day. Try a short morning rehearsal: breakfast, getting dressed and leaving the house at the same time each day.

- Pack the school bag together the night before
- Let your child choose their water bottle or lunch box
- Keep mornings calm and unhurried
sections.caption: A bright, open space to explore helps new children feel at home.

sections.heading: Keep goodbyes short and warm
sections.text: A hug, a clear goodbye and a promise of when you will be back works better than slipping away. Children settle faster when they know what to expect, and teachers are used to helping with first-day tears.

sections.heading: Celebrate the small wins
sections.text: Ask about the day with open questions such as **“What made you smile today?”** and celebrate every small step, from saying hello to a new friend to trying a new activity.

quote.text: Children settle faster when they know what to expect.

takeaways: Talk about preschool positively and often
Start the school-day routine a week or two early
Say a short, warm goodbye and come back on time
Celebrate every small step

title: Why play is serious learning
summary: Children under five learn best by seeing and doing. Here is what is really happening when a preschooler plays.
coverAlt: A bright indoor play area with rockers and slides on green turf
intro: To a grown-up, it can look like a child is simply playing. Look closer and you will see a scientist testing ideas, an engineer building, a storyteller practising new words and a team player learning to take turns.

sections.heading: Learning through the senses
sections.text: Children under five understand the world best through what they see, touch and do. Hands-on Montessori materials let them learn through their senses, at their own pace, and what they learn this way stays with them.
sections.caption: Picture cards turn new words into something children can see and hold.

sections.heading: Big skills from small games
sections.text: Stacking blocks builds early maths and patience. Pretend play builds language and empathy. Group games build problem-solving, communication and teamwork, the real-life skills that prepare children for what comes next.

sections.heading: Moving bodies, growing minds
sections.text: Movement matters too. Dance, yoga and outdoor play strengthen the body, improve balance and coordination, and help children focus when it is time to sit and listen.
sections.caption: Yoga and movement help little bodies and minds find their balance.

sections.heading: How to play along at home
sections.text: You don’t need special toys. Follow your child’s interests, ask open questions (“What happens if…?”), and give them time to try things their own way before stepping in.

quote.text: Children under five learn best by seeing and doing.

title: Five simple ways to build a love of reading at home
summary: Reading together for a few minutes a day does more than any app. Five easy habits that make books a favourite part of the day.
coverAlt: A teacher showing a picture card to a group of children
intro: A love of reading starts long before a child can read on their own. These five habits take only a few minutes a day.

sections.heading: Make it a daily ritual
sections.text: Pick a regular time, such as after dinner or just before bed, and read together every day, even if only for five minutes.

sections.heading: Let your child choose
sections.text: Children read more when they pick the book. Read the same favourite again and again; repetition builds vocabulary and confidence.

sections.heading: Talk about the pictures
sections.text: Point, ask and wonder together: “What do you think happens next?” “How does the bear feel?” Talking about a story matters as much as reading the words.

sections.heading: Keep books within reach
sections.text: A low shelf or a basket of books in the living room invites children to pick one up on their own.

sections.heading: Be a reading role model
sections.text: When children see the grown-ups around them reading, they learn that books are for everyone, not just for school.

takeaways: Read together every day, even briefly
Let your child choose (and repeat) favourites
Talk about the story and the pictures
Keep books where little hands can reach them

title: Choosing a preschool: what to look for and what to ask
summary: Visiting preschools? What to look for in the rooms, the questions worth asking, and why your own gut feeling counts.
coverAlt: A teacher kneels on a rainbow floor mat with three young children, matching picture cards of fruit and vegetables in a bright classroom
intro: A three-year-old kneels by a low shelf, chooses a tray of wooden pegs and carries it, very carefully, to a mat. Nobody told her to. Small moments like this tell you more about a preschool than any brochure, and you only see them by visiting, so here is what to look for and what to ask when you do.

sections.heading: Start with safety and hygiene
sections.text:
Most of this you can check with your own eyes. Walk through the rooms slowly, and look at them from a child's height as well as your own.

- Who can come in, and how does the school check who collects each child?
- Are sockets covered, sharp corners softened and heavy shelves fixed to the wall?
- Are the toilets and wash basins child-sized, clean and easy to reach?
- Where does drinking water come from, and where is food kept and served?
- Are staff trained in first aid, and what happens if a child falls ill during the day?

Don't feel awkward asking to see the toilets or the eating area. A good school will be glad you asked.

sections.heading: Watch how the day is spent
sections.text:
Ask for a typical day, then see whether the rooms match it. Young children need a steady rhythm: time to move, time to sit and listen, time to eat and rest, and plenty of time to play.

- What does a morning look like, from arrival to home time?
- How much time do children spend outdoors or moving about, and what happens on rainy days?
- Is there a quiet corner for a child who needs a break?
- How are snack times handled? Do children learn to open their own tiffin boxes, serve themselves and wash their hands?

Look at the walls too. Children's own drawings, each a little different, say more than rows of identical crafts that a grown-up clearly finished.

sections.heading: Look for play, not piles of worksheets
sections.text:
Children under five learn best by seeing and doing. Counting buttons into a bowl, pouring water from one jug to another, or building a tower that falls and trying again teaches more than tracing numbers on a sheet.

Ask how the school introduces early letters and numbers. Listen for words like **hands-on**, **materials**, **themes** and **projects**. If a three-year-old brings home written homework every day, ask why.

It is fair to want your child ready for big school. Good play-based learning gets them there: it builds concentration, language, the hand strength they will need for writing, and the confidence to have a go.
sections.caption: Wooden alphabet blocks spelling out PLAY. At this age, simple hands-on materials teach more than worksheets.

sections.heading: Ask about the teachers
sections.text:
Warm, unhurried teachers matter more than anything else on this list. Watch how they speak to children. Do they kneel to a child's eye level, use names and wait for the answer? Do they stay calm with a child who is upset?

Questions worth asking:

- How many children are in each class, and how many adults are with them through the day?
- What training do the teachers and helpers have?
- How long have most of the staff been here?
- Who does a child go to when they are hurt or sad?

Rather than looking for one magic number, ask the school to explain its class sizes and adult-to-child ratios, and why they suit each age. Then check that what you hear matches what you see in the room.

sections.heading: Ask how settling in works
sections.text:
Starting preschool is a big change, and most children need time. Ask how the first week or two are planned.

- Can a parent or grandparent stay for part of the first few days?
- Do new children start with shorter hours?
- How will the teacher let you know how your child is coping?
- What happens when a child cries at drop-off?

A school with a clear, gentle plan that doesn't rush you or your child understands that children settle and learn at their own pace.
sections.caption: A small child kneels on a soft rug, playing with a red toy truck. Time for free play helps a new place feel familiar.

sections.heading: Find out how the school talks to parents
sections.text:
You will be handing over your child for several hours a day, so you need to know what happens in that time.

- How will I hear about my child's day: a diary, an app, a quick chat at pick-up?
- How often do parents and teachers meet?
- If something goes wrong, how soon will I be told, and by whom?
- Is there CCTV, and who is allowed to see it?

Open, honest schools answer these easily. At Crossmaze, for example, families have a parents' app, and day-care parents can see a live CCTV view. Whatever the school, if an answer feels vague, ask again.

sections.heading: Trust your gut feeling
sections.text:
Before you leave, stand quietly in a classroom for five minutes. Are the children busy and absorbed? Is there a happy hum, rather than silence or chaos? Do they turn to their teachers easily? Can you picture your own child here?

You know your child best. If a place looks perfect on paper but doesn't feel right, that feeling counts. If it does feel right, that counts too.

We'd love you to bring this list to a Crossmaze centre. Book a visit to one of our five centres in Electronic City and Begur, look around for yourself, and ask us every question on it.

quote.text: You know your child best. If a place looks perfect on paper but doesn't feel right, that feeling counts.

takeaways: Check safety and hygiene with your own eyes
Look for hands-on play, not stacks of worksheets
Ask about class sizes and ratios, and watch the teachers
Look for a gentle settling-in plan and open, honest communication
Trust how the room feels

title: Screens and little ones: a calm, guilt-free guide
summary: What the WHO actually recommends for under-fives, plus easy swaps, screen-free zones and rainy-day ideas for a busy Indian home.
coverAlt: A group of smiling young children sitting together on stone steps outside a house with a blue wooden door
intro: It is late afternoon, it has been raining since lunch, the pressure cooker is whistling and your three-year-old wants one more video. If that sounds familiar, you are not alone, and this is not a guide to feeling guilty. It is a handful of small, realistic changes that make screens a smaller part of the day.

sections.heading: What the guidance actually says
sections.text:
In 2019 the World Health Organization published guidelines on physical activity, sedentary behaviour and sleep for children under five. On screens, they are short and clear:

- **Under 1 year:** screen time is not recommended.
- **1 year:** sedentary screen time, such as watching TV or videos or playing computer games, is not recommended.
- **2 to 4 years:** no more than one hour a day of sedentary screen time, and less is better.

The same guidelines encourage reading and storytelling with a caregiver whenever a young child is sitting still. Think of the hour as a ceiling, not a target.

These guidelines cover children under five, so they give no number for five- and six-year-olds. The same spirit is a sensible guide, and your paediatrician can help you decide what suits your child.

sections.heading: Swap, don't just switch off
sections.text:
Taking a screen away leaves a gap, and a bored toddler will fill it loudly. It works better to have something ready to put in its place:

- **Instead of a video at breakfast:** let your child help by counting idlis onto plates or stirring the batter.
- **Instead of cartoons while you cook:** a small ball of chapati dough of their own to roll, poke and shape beside you.
- **Instead of a phone in the car:** play I spy with colours, count red buses or sing the rhymes they know.
- **Instead of a tablet at the clinic:** a small pouch with a board book, a notepad and two chunky crayons.
- **Instead of a show to wind down:** the same short story every night. Repetition is comforting at this age.

sections.heading: Make some places screen-free
sections.text:
Rules about places are easier to keep than rules about minutes, because nobody has to watch the clock. Two good places to start:

- **Meal times.** Without a screen, a meal becomes a time to taste, chat and notice when the tummy is full. A plate of dal and rice eaten slowly, with the family talking, teaches a lot.
- **Bedrooms.** Keep TVs, tablets and phones out of the room where your child sleeps, and switch screens off a while before bed so the evening can slow down.

sections.heading: When the screen is on, sit with them
sections.text:
Some screen time is part of modern family life. When it happens, a few habits make it gentler:

1. Choose slow, simple programmes with a real story over fast, noisy ones, and turn off autoplay.
2. Watch together when you can, and talk about it: **“Why do you think the elephant looked sad?”**
3. Agree on the end before you start, such as two episodes and then hand-washing for dinner, and give a five-minute warning.
4. Prefer the living-room TV to a phone held close to the face, so it stays a shared, visible activity.

sections.heading: Bring grandparents and helpers along
sections.text:
In many homes, children spend long hours with grandparents or a nanny while parents work. Screens often appear because they are the easiest way through a long afternoon, not because anyone is careless. Talk it through kindly rather than handing over a list of rules:

- Explain the why, and share the WHO guidance in your own words.
- Ask for their ideas. Grandparents often know more rhymes, stories and games than any app.
- Leave easy options within reach: a basket of books, some play-dough, a ball.
- Agree on one or two rules everyone keeps, such as no screens at meals.

Many families see a video call with a grandparent who lives far away as different from cartoons, because the child is talking and listening to someone they love. That is your family's choice to make.

sections.heading: Children copy what they see
sections.text:
Little ones watch us far more closely than they watch any screen. If they see a parent scrolling at the dinner table, they learn that phones belong there. Try leaving your own phone in another room during meals and for the first hour after you come home.

When you do pick it up, say what you are doing: **“I'm checking when Ajji's bus arrives.”** It shows that a phone is a tool you use for a reason, then put down.

sections.heading: A rainy afternoon without the tablet
sections.text:
Bengaluru's rain can keep everyone indoors for hours. Keep this list on the fridge:

1. **Paper boats.** Fold them together, then float them in a bucket of water. Stay right beside your child; even a little water needs an adult close by.
2. **Kitchen band.** Steel plates, wooden spoons and a shaker made from a small box of rice, taped firmly shut. March and sing.
3. **Painting.** Spread old newspaper on the floor and paint with fingers or a thick brush, using washable, child-safe paints.
4. **Bedsheet fort.** Drape a sheet over two chairs to make a cave for reading by torchlight.
5. **Rain watching.** Sit by the window, race the drops down the glass and name the sounds you hear.
6. **Animal yoga.** Be a cat, a cobra, then a tree, holding each pose for three slow breaths.

Keep small things such as beads and dry beans away from under-threes, as they can cause choking. Keep button batteries well out of reach of all young children: the NHS warns they can cause severe internal burns if swallowed.
sections.caption: Children's paint-covered hands over a shared sheet of paper. Messy, hands-on play can fill a long indoor afternoon.

sections.heading: Be kind to yourself
sections.text:
Some days will have more screen time than you planned: a fever, a work deadline, a long journey. That is normal. What matters is the pattern across weeks, not one hard afternoon. Pick one change from this list, try it for a week, and add another when it feels easy.

At Crossmaze, our Montessori-based approach is built on visual, practical, hands-on learning, because children under five learn best by seeing and doing. The same is true at home: a lump of dough, a stack of blocks and a grown-up who joins in go a long way.

quote.text: Think of the hour as a ceiling, not a target.

takeaways: Under two: no sedentary screen time, says the WHO
Two to four: an hour a day at most, less is better
Keep meals and bedrooms screen-free
Have a swap ready before you switch off
Watch together, and model the habits you want

title: Happy mealtimes with a choosy eater
summary: Calm, no-pressure ideas for the child who pushes the beans to the side: small portions, eating together and a colourful thali.
coverAlt: Folded chapatis beside a mixed vegetable sambar in a steel plate
intro: The dal is going cold, the chapati has been torn into twenty pieces and not one has been eaten. If mealtimes with your little one feel like a daily tug of war, you are not alone, and a calmer table usually helps more than a cleverer trick.

sections.heading: Take the pressure off
sections.text:
Choosy eating is common in the toddler and preschool years. The NHS, the UK's health service, says it is perfectly normal for toddlers to refuse new foods, and that it helps to look at what your child eats over a week rather than in a single day. Tastes change, too.

A helpful way to share the job: **you decide what is served, when and where; your child decides whether to eat it and how much.** This idea, called the division of responsibility, comes from the American dietitian Ellyn Satter. It lets you stop counting mouthfuls and lets your child listen to their own hunger.

sections.heading: Small portions, offered again and again
sections.text:
A full plate can look like a mountain to a three-year-old. Start with a spoonful of each thing and let them ask for more.

If a food is refused, don't make a fuss and don't give up on it. The NHS says it may take lots of attempts before a child accepts some foods. Put two or three green peas or a thin slice of carrot on the plate again next week, and the week after. Touching, smelling and licking a food all count as progress.
sections.caption: Crinkle-cut carrot, sweetcorn and peas laid out as a flower on a white plate

sections.heading: Serve a familiar food alongside a new one
sections.text:
New foods feel safer next to old friends. Put a little of something new beside a food your child already enjoys, so there is always something on the plate they are happy to eat.

- A spoon of beans palya next to their favourite curd rice
- A small piece of beetroot or palak chapati beside a plain one
- One mini idli with a new chutney, and the usual sambar too

sections.heading: Eat together when you can
sections.text:
Children copy what they see. The NHS calls copying you the best way for a child to learn to enjoy new foods. When parents, grandparents or older cousins sit down and eat the same food, a child is more likely to try it than when they eat alone.

You don't need a family dinner every night. Even one shared meal a day, or a weekend breakfast of dosa together, gives your child a chance to watch you eat, talk about the food and see that new tastes are nothing to worry about.
sections.caption: A parent offers a spoonful to a little one in a high chair. Sharing the table, even briefly, makes meals feel sociable.

sections.heading: Let them wash, mix and help
sections.text:
Children are much more curious about food they have touched. Give your little one a real job in the kitchen:

- Wash tomatoes or rinse spinach leaves in a bowl of water
- Tear coriander or curry leaves
- Stir curd into rice, or mix a dosa topping
- Roll a small ball of chapati dough

At Crossmaze we believe children under five learn best by seeing and doing, and the kitchen is a lovely place for it. **Safety first:** keep little hands away from the stove, hot oil, pressure cookers and knives, and stay beside them the whole time.

sections.heading: No bribes, no screens at the table
sections.text:
"Two more bites and you can have a chocolate" can work tonight, but it teaches that vegetables are a chore and sweets are the prize. The NHS advises against using food as a reward; a trip to the park or a game together works better.

Screens are tempting too, because a child watching cartoons will open their mouth without thinking. But a distracted child is less likely to notice the taste, or when they are full. Keep phones and the TV off at meals, for grown-ups as well, and talk about the food instead: its colour, its crunch, where it came from.

sections.heading: Keep regular meal and snack times
sections.text:
A child who has been nibbling biscuits all afternoon won't be hungry for dinner. The NHS suggests three meals a day for young children, with up to two healthy snacks in between. A simple, regular rhythm like this helps your child come to the table hungry.

Good snacks can be simple: a banana, a few pieces of guava, a small bowl of poha or a slice of chapati with ghee. **Choking safety:** the NHS advises cutting small, round foods such as grapes and cherry tomatoes into quarters, and not giving whole nuts to children under five. Have your child sit down to eat, and stay with them while they do.

sections.heading: Make a colourful thali
sections.text:
A steel thali with small katoris turns a meal into a little adventure. Fill a few with bright, simple foods and let your child choose where to start.

- Orange: steamed carrot sticks or a piece of pumpkin
- Green: cucumber slices or a spoon of peas
- Yellow: dal or a little lemon rice
- White: curd or a mini idli
- Red: pomegranate seeds or beetroot

Name the colours together and count the katoris. Some days your child will only eat the yellow ones, and that is fine. Exploring is part of learning, and every child gets there at their own pace.

sections.heading: When to talk to your paediatrician
sections.text:
Most choosy eating is a phase, but do speak to your child's paediatrician if:

- They are losing weight, or you are worried about their growth
- They eat only a very small number of foods, or are dropping foods they used to eat
- They often gag, choke or have trouble chewing or swallowing
- They seem unwell or very tired, or mealtimes cause them real distress

Your doctor can check their growth and tell you whether anything more is needed. If you are unsure, it is always fine to ask.

quote.text: Touching, smelling and licking a food all count as progress.

takeaways: Keep the table calm and pressure-free
Offer small portions, and offer new foods again and again
Eat together and let your child help in the kitchen
No bribes and no screens at meals
Ask your paediatrician if you are worried about weight or growth

title: Safe and unsafe touch: talking to young children about body safety
summary: Simple, calm words and everyday habits that help children aged two to six understand body safety and know they can always tell you.
coverAlt: A small child walking between two adults and holding both their hands, seen from behind on a sunny road
intro: Bath time, a cuddle with a cousin, a visit to the doctor: everyday moments give us easy ways to teach children about their bodies. Body safety doesn't need one big, scary talk. It grows from small, calm conversations that tell your child their body belongs to them and they can always tell you anything.

sections.heading: Start with the right words
sections.text:
Teach the real names for every part of the body, private parts included, in the same matter-of-fact voice you use for elbow or knee. The UK children's charity NSPCC, in its PANTS guide for parents, says it is good to use the correct names if you are comfortable doing so. A child who has the words can tell you clearly if something is wrong, and words said without embarrassment send a quiet message: this is not a shameful subject, and you can talk to me about it.

Pet names are sweet, but they can confuse a teacher, a doctor or a grandparent who is trying to understand what a child means. Bath time and getting dressed are natural moments to practise.

sections.heading: The swimsuit rule
sections.text:
A simple way to explain private parts is the swimsuit rule: **the parts of your body that a swimsuit covers are private.** The Council of Europe's Underwear Rule and the NSPCC's PANTS guide use the same idea, with underwear in place of a swimsuit. Explain it plainly:

- Nobody should touch your private parts, or ask to see them
- Nobody should ask you to touch or look at theirs
- Nobody should show you pictures or videos of private parts

Then explain the exceptions, so the rule makes sense in real life. While your child is small, mum, dad or a carer you have chosen may help with washing or the toilet. A doctor or nurse may need to check, with mum or dad there; they should explain why and ask first.

You can describe a **safe touch** as one that feels kind and okay, like a high five, holding hands to cross the road, or a hug they wanted. An **unsafe touch** is one that hurts, feels confusing or uncomfortable, touches private parts, or comes with a request to keep it secret. Make it clear that the rule is the same for everyone, including people your child knows and loves.

sections.heading: Surprises, not secrets
sections.text:
Young children find the difference between a surprise and a secret easy to grasp. A surprise is something happy that everyone finds out soon, like a birthday present for Appa or a cake for Ajji. A secret is something someone tells you never to share.

Make it a family rule: **we have surprises, not secrets.** If any grown-up or older child ever asks your child to keep a secret from you, they should tell you, and they will never be in trouble for it. This one habit takes away a tool that people who harm children often rely on.

sections.heading: Hugs are a choice
sections.text:
Consent starts with everyday affection. If your child doesn't want to hug an uncle at a family function or sit on a neighbour's lap, let them say no. Offer another way to greet people: a wave, a namaste or a high five. It can feel awkward in front of relatives, but a quiet word to grandparents beforehand usually helps.

Practise both sides. Stop tickling the moment your child says stop, and ask before you hug them now and then. Teach them to ask a friend, "Can I hug you?" and to accept a no. Children whose no is respected at home learn that their voice counts.

sections.heading: Choose trusted adults together
sections.text:
Help your child name three to five grown-ups they could go to if they felt unsafe or worried: perhaps mum and dad, a grandparent, an aunt, and their class teacher. Count them on one hand together. Remind your child that if one adult doesn't listen, they should keep telling the next one until someone helps.

Practise saying no in a strong, clear voice, then walking away and telling. A little role-play makes it feel like a skill rather than a fear: "What would you do if someone asked you to keep a secret?"
sections.caption: A grown-up and a small child walking hand in hand along a path beside the grass, seen from behind.

sections.heading: What to say at each age
sections.text:
Keep it short, repeat it often and go at your child's pace.

- **Two to three:** name the body parts at bath time, use "stop means stop" during play, and say "your body belongs to you"
- **Three to four:** introduce the swimsuit rule and the difference between surprises and secrets, and name trusted adults together
- **Four to six:** role-play saying no and telling, talk about touches that feel confusing, and remind them that rules about bodies apply to everyone, even people they know

sections.heading: If your child tells you something
sections.text:
How you react in the first few minutes matters most. Stay as calm as you can, even if you feel shaken inside.

1. Listen, and let your child use their own words
2. Believe them, and tell them so
3. Thank them for telling you, and say it is not their fault
4. Don't press them with lots of questions or promise to keep it secret
5. Get help the same day

In India, you can call the free Child Helpline on 1098, day or night. If a child is in danger right now, call 112, the national emergency number. Talk to your paediatrician too; they can check your child and point you to the right support.

sections.heading: Keep the conversation going
sections.text:
Body safety works best as a quiet thread through ordinary days, not a single lecture. Read a picture book about feelings, ask "How did that make you feel?" after a playdate, and notice when your child speaks up for themselves.

A good preschool will be happy to talk to you about how it keeps children safe. At Crossmaze we want every child to feel cherished and respected, and we are happy to answer your questions about safety when you visit.

quote.text: Children whose no is respected at home learn that their voice counts.

takeaways: Use the real names for all body parts
Teach the swimsuit rule, with its exceptions
Have surprises, not secrets
Let hugs be a choice
Stay calm, believe your child and get help

title: Big feelings, little people: helping children name and manage emotions
summary: Meltdowns are a normal part of growing up. Calm, simple ways to help children aged 2 to 6 name their feelings and find their way back to calm.
coverAlt: Close-up of a small child’s hand holding an adult’s finger, with blurred green trees behind
intro: The block tower falls, and a happy three-year-old turns into a storm of tears and stamping feet. Moments like this happen in every home and classroom. They are not a sign that anything is wrong; they are a chance to teach a skill your child will use for life.

sections.heading: Why little storms happen
sections.text:
Young children feel things fully, but the part of them that says “wait, let’s think about this” is still being built. Harvard University’s Center on the Developing Child explains that the skills behind self-control start to develop soon after birth, grow especially fast between about three and five years old, and keep developing through the teenage years into early adulthood.

So when a two-year-old melts down because the banana broke in half, or a five-year-old storms off after losing a game, they are not being naughty. Their feelings have simply run ahead of their skills. Our job is not to stop the feelings but to lend children our calm and, bit by bit, teach them what to do next.

Know the usual triggers too: hunger, tiredness, too much noise and sudden changes, such as leaving the park or turning off a cartoon. A snack, a rest or a five-minute warning prevents more storms than clever words afterwards.

sections.heading: Give the feeling a name
sections.text:
Children can’t manage a feeling they have no words for. Naming it out loud, without judging it, is the first step: **“You’re really angry that the tower fell.”** It shows you understand, and slowly gives them words to use themselves.

It changes with age:

- **2 to 3 years:** keep to a few simple words such as happy, sad, angry and scared, and say what you see: “You’re sad. Appa has gone to work.”
- **3 to 4 years:** add words like frustrated, worried, excited and disappointed, and link them to a reason: “You’re frustrated because the zip is stuck.”
- **4 to 6 years:** start asking instead of telling: “How did your body feel when that happened?” Children this age can begin to notice clues such as a hot face or tight fists.

Use your home language too: feelings words in Kannada, Tamil, Hindi or English all count, and grandparents can join in.

sections.heading: Stay close, stay calm
sections.text:
In the middle of a meltdown, a child is too upset to take in a lesson. This is the moment to say less and be there more.

- Get down to your child’s level and keep your voice low and slow
- Offer a hug, or simply sit nearby if they don’t want to be touched
- Keep everyone safe: move breakable things and gently stop hitting or throwing
- Hold the limit kindly: “I won’t let you hit. You can stamp your feet instead.”

Your calm rubs off on your child, and so does your stress. If your own temper rises, take a slow breath first. Saying “I need a moment to calm down too” shows your child exactly what calming down looks like.

If parents and grandparents share the care, agree together on the same few words and the same response.

sections.heading: A calm corner and a few breathing games
sections.text:
A calm corner is a cosy spot to settle down: a comfort, not a punishment. A floor cushion, a favourite soft toy and two or three picture books are enough. Set it up together on a happy day so it feels like your child’s own.

Slow breathing can help the body settle, and children learn it best as a game. Practise when everyone is relaxed, so it is ready when feelings run high:

1. **Smell the flower, blow the candle:** breathe in through the nose as if smelling a flower, then breathe out slowly as if blowing out a birthday candle.
2. **Teddy ride:** lie down with a soft toy on the tummy and watch it rise and fall with each slow breath.
3. **Bubble breath:** pretend to blow one big, slow bubble without popping it.
4. **Hissing snake:** breathe in, then let the air out in a long, quiet “ssss”.

Keep it to three or four breaths, and do them with your child rather than telling them to.
sections.caption: A favourite soft toy is a simple start for a calm corner, and a breathing buddy too.

sections.heading: Feelings faces, drawings and stories
sections.text:
Children learn about feelings most easily when they are not in the middle of one, so use calm, playful moments.

- **Feelings faces:** draw simple happy, sad, angry and scared faces on paper plates or cards. Ask your child to point to the one that matches how they feel, or how a character in a story feels.
- **Draw it out:** older children can draw a time they felt cross or proud and tell you about it.
- **Picture books:** pause on a page and wonder aloud: “How do you think she feels? What could she do?” Stories let children try out big feelings from a safe distance.

This is learning by seeing and doing at its simplest, and children under five learn best that way.
sections.caption: Drawing gives children a way to show a feeling they can’t yet put into words.

sections.heading: After the storm
sections.text:
Once your child is calm, reconnect before you teach. A cuddle, a sip of water and a quiet “That was a big feeling, wasn’t it?” mend the moment. Then talk briefly about what might help next time. With a two-year-old that might be one sentence; a five-year-old can help you make a plan.

Praise the effort, not only the result: **“You took three big breaths and calmed your body. That was hard, and you did it.”** Children repeat what we notice.

Progress is slow and uneven, and every child learns at their own pace. At Crossmaze, celebrating every milestone, big or small, is one of our core values, and learning to calm down after a big feeling is one of the big milestones of the early years. Notice the small wins at home too.

If meltdowns are very frequent or very long, if your child often hurts themselves or others, or if you are simply worried, talk to your paediatrician about what is typical for your child.

quote.text: Our job is not to stop the feelings but to lend children our calm.

takeaways: Meltdowns are normal: feelings grow faster than self-control
Name the feeling out loud, without judging it
Stay close, speak softly and keep everyone safe
Practise breathing games when everyone is calm
Reconnect first, then praise the effort

title: Learning hides in everyday moments at home
summary: Pouring water, counting idlis, matching socks: simple jobs at home that build maths, language and independence, with ideas for ages 2 to 6.
coverAlt: A young child's hands holding a fresh pea pod, with more pods resting on their lap
intro: Watch a two-year-old pour water from a small jug into a steel tumbler: the tongue pokes out, the whole body goes still, and a little splash lands on the tray. That is real learning, and your home is full of moments like it.

sections.heading: Why small jobs are big learning
sections.text:
Pouring, sorting, wiping and carrying look like simple chores to us. To a young child they are puzzles to solve with hands, eyes and the whole body. Maria Montessori called this kind of work practical life, and it is still a core part of Montessori classrooms today.

Each small job quietly builds something:

- **Fine motor control:** pouring, pinching pegs and shelling peas work the same small hand muscles a child will later use to hold a crayon and a pencil
- **Early maths:** counting, matching, and sorting by colour or size
- **Language:** new words for what they see, touch and smell
- **Concentration:** a task with a clear beginning and end holds attention
- **Independence:** the quiet pride of “I did it myself”

At Crossmaze, learning is Montessori-based, practical and hands-on, because children under five learn best by seeing and doing. Home is a natural place to keep that going.

sections.heading: In the kitchen
sections.text:
The kitchen is full of real work, and children love real work.

- **Pouring:** put a small steel jug with a little water and a tumbler on a tray. Spills are part of the lesson, so keep a cloth nearby and show how to wipe up
- **Counting idlis:** “How many idlis for Appa? How many for you?” Count them onto the plates, then count again as they disappear
- **Sorting vegetables:** potatoes in one basket, onions in another, tomatoes in a third. Ask which is the heaviest, the smoothest, the biggest
- **Washing and picking:** rinsing fruit, shelling peas or picking coriander leaves off the stalks is slow, satisfying work for busy fingers

Talk while you cook. Name what you are doing (“I’m stirring the dal”, “Look, the chapati is puffing up”), ask what they can smell, and let them guess what comes next. This easy running chatter is one of the simplest ways to give a child new words.
sections.caption: A small hand reaching for strawberries on a chopping board by the kitchen sink. Rinsing fruit is a good first kitchen job.

sections.heading: Around the house
sections.text:
- **Laundry by colour:** before clothes go into the machine, sort them into piles of whites, darks and colours. Later, hunt for everything blue
- **Matching socks:** a basket of clean socks is a ready-made matching game. Pair them, count the pairs and find the odd one out
- **Laying the table:** one plate, one tumbler and one spoon for each person. It is counting with a purpose, and it tells a child they are helping the family
- **Putting things back:** a low shelf or basket for toys and shoes means a child can tidy up without help

Grandparents at home are often wonderful at this: patient, unhurried and full of stories to tell while the work gets done.

sections.heading: Balcony, garden and the shops
sections.text:
- **Watering plants:** a small mug or watering can, one pot at a time. Talk about which plant looks thirsty and how the soil changes after a Bengaluru shower
- **Counting steps:** count the stairs up to your flat or the steps to the gate. Count backwards on the way down for a challenge
- **A picture shopping list:** draw or cut out pictures of tomatoes, bananas and milk. Your child holds the list and ticks off each item at the shop
- **Noticing:** the colours at the vegetable cart, the numbers on the gates, the shapes of leaves on the walk home
sections.caption: A child pressing soil around a young plant. Looking after plants teaches patience and gentle hands.

sections.heading: Ideas by age
sections.text:
Every child learns at their own pace, so treat these as starting points rather than milestones.

**Two to three years**

- Pour water between two small jugs over a tray
- Put spoons in the drawer and socks in the basket
- Name vegetables as you unpack the shopping
- Water one plant with a small mug

**Three to four years**

- Sort laundry or vegetables by colour
- Match socks and count the pairs
- Count idlis, chapatis or stairs up to ten
- Lay the table for two or three people

**Four to six years**

- Help plan a meal and make a picture shopping list
- Share things out fairly: “Six biscuits, three people. How many each?”
- Measure rice or dal with a cup for cooking
- Look after a plant of their own and notice how it changes each week

sections.heading: Keeping it safe and calm
sections.text:
- Stay close whenever water is involved, and never leave a small child alone with a bucket or tub of water
- Keep little ones away from the hob, hot pans, pressure cookers and sharp knives
- Choose objects too big to fit in a small child's mouth, and watch closely when food is part of the job. The American Academy of Pediatrics advises keeping high-risk foods such as whole grapes, nuts, popcorn and chunks of raw vegetable or fruit away from children until at least age four
- Keep cleaning products and medicines out of reach, even when your child is “helping”
- Go slowly and expect some mess. A job done imperfectly with pride is worth more than one done perfectly by you

If you are unsure what suits your child, talk to your paediatrician.

quote.text: A job done imperfectly with pride is worth more than one done perfectly by you.

takeaways: Everyday jobs build hands, maths, words and focus
Start small: one job, one tray, a few minutes
Talk as you work to give your child new words
Match the job to your child's age and stay close

title: Kindness, sharing and taking turns: helping little ones get along
summary: Why “mine!” is a normal stage, why turn-taking comes before sharing, and calm, simple ways to grow kindness in children aged 2 to 6.
coverAlt: Brightly coloured wooden building blocks scattered across a soft beige rug
intro: Two cousins, one red truck, and suddenly the whole family function can hear about it. Squabbles over toys are a normal part of growing up. With patience and a few simple habits, children slowly learn to wait, take turns, share and care about how others feel.

sections.heading: Why “mine!” comes first
sections.text:
Around the age of two, children are busy working out that they are a separate person, with their own things. Saying “mine!” and holding on tight is part of that discovery, not a sign of a selfish child. Little ones also live very much in the moment. “Later” means little to a two-year-old, so giving up the truck now seems like giving it up completely.

This changes with time and practice. The American Academy of Pediatrics’ HealthyChildren.org explains that once children reach three, they are usually much less self-centred, and when they play in small groups they learn to share toys and take turns. Many three-year-olds can even sort out a quarrel by taking turns or swapping toys, though grown-ups still need to encourage this, especially at first.

So go gently with your expectations. Sharing is a skill to be learnt, like using a spoon, and nobody gets it right on the first day.

sections.heading: Take turns before you share
sections.text:
Turn-taking is easier to understand than sharing, because the toy always comes back. Start there.

- Play simple **“your turn, my turn”** games: rolling a ball back and forth, adding one block each to a tower, or pouring water from a jug in turns at bath time.
- Use a timer for a much-loved toy. A sand timer or a kitchen timer makes waiting easier to see: “When the sand runs out, it’s Arjun’s turn.”
- Give the waiting child something to do: “While you wait, shall we fill the truck with these blocks?”
- Keep turns short for two-year-olds. A minute feels very long when you are little.

Older children enjoy easy board games with big dice and a few pieces, where they can practise waiting, winning and losing kindly. Keep small pieces, beads and marbles away from children under three, and stay close whenever little ones play with small objects.
sections.caption: A heap of brightly coloured wooden game pieces. Simple board games are a gentle way to practise waiting for a turn.

sections.heading: Notice kindness, and show it
sections.text:
Children repeat what we notice. When you see a kind moment, name it plainly: **“You gave Ajji the first piece of your dosa. That was kind.”** Or: **“You waited for your turn on the swing. That was hard, and you did it.”** Specific words teach more than a quick “good boy” or “good girl”.

Children also watch what we do far more closely than they listen to what we say. Everyday life gives plenty of chances to show kindness:

- Share your own things out loud: “Would you like some of my orange? Let’s have half each.”
- Say thank you often, to your child and to others, from the auto driver to the vegetable seller.
- Let your child help: carrying a plate of sweets to the neighbours at Deepavali, or setting out water for the grandparents.
- Ask about tiffin time: what did you share today, and what did a friend share with you?

When children see the adults around them taking turns to talk, making room for each other and saying sorry, kindness starts to feel normal.

sections.heading: Stories and pretend play grow empathy
sections.text:
Caring about how someone else feels starts with noticing that they have feelings at all. Stories and pretend play let children practise this safely.

While you read a picture book, pause and wonder aloud: “Look at his face. How do you think he feels? What could his friend do?” A grandparent’s stories, from the Panchatantra or from their own childhood, work just as well.

Pretend play does the same job. Your child might feed a hungry teddy, put a sleepy doll to bed or bandage a soft toy’s sore paw. Join in and add a small problem: “Oh no, Bunny has no plate. What shall we do?” Then let your child find the kind answer.
sections.caption: A teddy bear sits on a red garden swing. Soft toys make patient partners for pretend play, and for practising turns.

sections.heading: When your child grabs or won’t share
sections.text:
Even with lots of practice, there will be snatching and tears. Stay calm and keep your words short.

1. **Step in early and gently.** Keep a hand on the toy if you need to: “I won’t let you grab. Riya is still using it.”
2. **Name both feelings.** “You really want the truck. Riya isn’t finished yet.”
3. **Offer a way forward.** A timer, a swap or another toy: “Let’s set the timer. Then it’s your turn.”
4. **Help the other child too.** Comfort the child whose toy was grabbed, and help both of them find their words.

Try not to make a child hand over a toy the moment another child asks for it. Waiting for a turn is a fair rule, and children learn more from it than from a grown-up deciding for them. Before visitors come, it is fine to put away one or two special things your child doesn’t want to share, and leave out toys that are easy for everyone to play with.

Skip the long lecture, and never shame a child in front of cousins or friends. A quiet word and a fresh start work better.

sections.heading: What to expect, age by age
sections.text:
Every child learns at their own pace, so think of this as a rough guide, not a checklist.

- **2 to 3 years:** plenty of “mine!”. Short, simple turns with an adult close by work best. Praise every small step.
- **3 to 4 years:** more interest in playing with other children. Many can wait for a short turn with a timer, swap toys and begin to notice when a friend is sad.
- **4 to 6 years:** children can make simple rules together, play board games, share a tiffin and start to sort out squabbles with a little help.

Preschool is a natural place to practise all of this. At Crossmaze, our thematic curriculum brings personal, social and emotional development together with language, thinking and movement, and in Junior KG, group activities encourage teamwork, sharing and taking turns. We build warm connections between children, parents and staff, and we celebrate every milestone, big or small, including the day a child hands over the red truck all by themselves.

quote.text: Sharing is a skill to be learnt, like using a spoon, and nobody gets it right on the first day.

takeaways: “Mine!” at two or three is a normal stage, not selfishness
Start with turn-taking; a timer makes waiting easier
Name kind acts when you see them, and show kindness at home
Use stories and pretend play to talk about feelings
When a toy is grabbed, stay calm, name feelings and offer a way forward

title: Healthy habits for the cold season: hand-washing, coughs and rest
summary: Simple, calm habits for the cooler months: washing hands well, covering coughs, enough sleep and knowing when to stay home.
coverAlt: Hands covered in soap foam under a running tap at a kitchen sink
intro: The mornings in Bengaluru are cooler, the sniffles are going round, and every little nose seems to be running. You can't keep every cold away, but a few small habits, practised calmly every day, help your child stay well and recover faster.

sections.heading: Make hand-washing a daily rhythm
sections.text:
Washing hands is the simplest habit on this list and one of the most useful. UNICEF says good hand hygiene helps protect children against illnesses such as pneumonia and diarrhoea, and it marks Global Handwashing Day every year on 15 October.

The trick is to make it part of the day, not a battle. Wash at the same moments every time, so your child stops asking why.

sections.heading: Wash for about as long as it takes to sing a song
sections.text:
The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) advises scrubbing with soap for at least 20 seconds, and suggests humming a tune twice through as a timer. A rhyme your child already loves works well.

1. Wet both hands under clean running water.
2. Add soap and rub palms, backs of hands, between fingers and under nails.
3. Rinse well.
4. Dry with a clean towel.

Stand beside your child at the basin, and keep a small stool there so they can reach the tap safely and wash on their own.

A gentle guide by age: two-year-olds need a grown-up's hands over theirs. Three-year-olds can lather and rinse with a little help. By four to six, most children can manage on their own while you watch and sing along. Always stay close to a child at a basin, as wet floors and tall stools are easy to slip from.
sections.caption: Hands rinsing under a thin stream of water. Rubbing every part of the hand, then rinsing well, matters as much as the soap.

sections.heading: Know the moments that count
sections.text:
According to the CDC, hands should be washed:

- before and after eating, and before and after preparing food
- after using the toilet or having a nappy changed
- after blowing the nose, coughing or sneezing
- after touching animals, pet food or rubbish
- before and after caring for someone who is sick

At home, add one more: as soon as your child comes in from outside, before they reach for a snack. Plain soap and water is best. The CDC says an alcohol-based sanitiser (at least 60% alcohol) is only for when soap and water are not available. If you use one, rub it on with an adult's help and keep the bottle out of little hands, because swallowing it is harmful.

sections.heading: Cough and sneeze into your elbow
sections.text:
Little ones cough straight into the air, or into their hands and then onto everything they touch. Teach a simple habit: **cough or sneeze into the bend of your elbow, or into a tissue, then wash your hands.**

Make it a game. Pretend to be a “sneezing elephant” who tucks the trunk into the elbow. Children copy what they see, so do it yourself too, and keep a box of tissues where your child can reach it.

If your child has a cold, show them how to bin the used tissue and then wash their hands, so the habit finishes properly.

sections.heading: Sleep is part of staying well
sections.text:
Tired bodies find it harder to cope. The World Health Organization's 2019 guidelines for children under 5 recommend 10 to 13 hours of good-quality sleep a day for children aged 3 to 4, and this can include a nap. They also ask for regular sleep and wake-up times.

In the cooler months, keep bedtime steady, dress your child in light layers rather than heavy ones, and have a calm wind-down with a story and low lights. Every child is different, so if you are worried about your child's sleep, talk to your paediatrician.
sections.caption: A small child asleep with their head on a white pillow. Regular, restful sleep helps little bodies cope with the cold season.

sections.heading: Keep the little things clean
sections.text:
Cold germs travel on shared things. The CDC recommends cleaning commonly touched surfaces regularly. At home that means door handles, light switches, the tap, and the tiffin box and water bottle, which should be washed with soap after every school day.

No need for anything fancy: warm water, soap and a clean cloth. Wash soft toys and your child's hand towel often, and give each child their own towel.

sections.heading: When your child is unwell, rest at home
sections.text:
The CDC says people who are sick should stay home and away from others to avoid spreading illness. A child with a fever or a heavy cough needs rest, plenty of fluids and quiet, and so do the other children around them.

If your child seems very unwell, or you are unsure, please see your paediatrician. They will tell you what is safe to give, and when your child is ready to return. Never give a child medicine without a doctor's advice. Letting your child's school know why they are away helps, too, so teachers can keep an eye on how the other children are doing.

quote.text: Wash at the same moments every day, and hand-washing stops being a battle and becomes a habit.

takeaways: Wash hands with soap for at least 20 seconds: sing a song to time it
Wash before eating, after the toilet and when coming in from outside
Teach coughing and sneezing into the elbow or a tissue
Keep bedtime regular: 10 to 13 hours a day for ages 3 to 4, nap included
Keep a sick child at home and ask your paediatrician when in doubt

title: Why a structured routine matters: 5 simple reasons
summary: Five simple reasons a steady daily routine helps children aged 2 to 6 feel safe, manage big feelings and grow in independence, at school and at home.
coverAlt: Children's hands covered in bright paint on a large sheet of paper
intro: Ask any preschool teacher what makes a good day, and they will often say: a good rhythm. Children between two and six are still learning how a day fits together, and a steady routine gives them that picture. Here are five simple reasons it matters, for school mornings and for home.

sections.heading: A routine tells your child what comes next
sections.text:
Young children don't read clocks, so the day can feel like a series of surprises. A steady order of events gives them a map: first we arrive, then we play, then we wash hands and eat. When children know what comes next, they stop spending energy on worrying and have more left for exploring.

This is why a classroom with a clear daily rhythm feels calm even with a dozen busy two- and three-year-olds in it. The same is true at home. You don't need a timetable on the wall. You need the same order, most days.

sections.heading: Routines make big feelings smaller
sections.text:
Many meltdowns happen at the moment of change: the cartoon ends, the park closes, it is time to leave. A child who knows the pattern, and gets a gentle warning, copes far better than one who is surprised.

- Give a five-minute warning: “Two more turns on the slide, then we go home.”
- Use the same words each time, such as “first shoes, then bag”
- Sing a short tidy-up song so the change has a signal
- Say what is coming next, not only what must stop

For a child who finds goodbyes hard, a small repeated ritual, such as a wave at the gate and a special phrase, becomes a comfort in itself. Some children will still cry, and that is normal. A predictable goodbye helps them settle faster.

sections.heading: Regular sleep, meals and play help little bodies
sections.text:
The World Health Organization recommends 10 to 13 hours of good-quality sleep a day for children aged 3 to 4, which may include a nap, with regular sleep and wake-up times. It also advises no more than one hour a day of sedentary screen time for children aged 2 to 4, and less is better.

A steady rhythm makes both easier. When breakfast, tiffin, lunch and bedtime come at roughly the same times, hunger and tiredness stop being daily surprises. Active play, outdoors when the Bengaluru weather allows, fits best in the same slots each day.

Every child is different, so if you are worried about your child's sleep, appetite or energy, talk to your paediatrician.
sections.caption: A child colouring with a box of crayons close by. A calm, regular drawing time builds focus.

sections.heading: Routines build independence and confidence
sections.text:
When the order of the day is familiar, children can start doing parts of it by themselves. They hang up the bag, wash hands, put on shoes, wipe the table. Each small job done without help brings the quiet pride of “I did it myself”.

This fits well with Montessori-based learning, which Crossmaze uses: children work with hands-on materials at their own pace, and take care of their own space. A predictable day gives that independence a safe frame.

At home, try a simple morning and evening pattern:

1. **Morning:** wake up, toilet, wash face, dress (with help for the buttons), breakfast, bag by the door
2. **Evening:** wash hands, snack, play, bath, dinner, two books, lights out

Choose which steps your child can do alone, and let them. It will take longer at first, but it is worth the extra minutes.

sections.heading: Home and school working together
sections.text:
Children settle best when the rhythm at home and at school feels like one story. Crossmaze's thematic curriculum brings language, numbers, social skills and physical development together in every theme. A clear rhythm at home supports that kind of steady learning, and you can build it in simple ways.

- **Ask about the day in the same order:** “What did you play? What did you eat? Who did you sit with?”
- **Keep the school-morning pattern the same** on most days, and a gentler version on holidays
- **Share what works.** Tell your child's teacher about any change at home, such as a new baby, a trip or a bad night. Small changes can show up as big feelings in class
- **Be flexible.** Fever, festivals and guests will change the day. Go back to the pattern as soon as you can, and your child will follow

A routine is a frame, not a cage. The aim is a child who feels safe, not a day run by the clock.
sections.caption: Coloured pencils lined up in a neat row. Order and rhythm help children feel secure.

quote.text: A routine is a frame, not a cage. The aim is a child who feels safe, not a day run by the clock.

takeaways: A steady order of events helps young children feel safe and know what comes next
Warnings and familiar words make changes and goodbyes easier
WHO advises 10 to 13 hours of sleep for ages 3 to 4, with regular sleep and wake-up times
Let children do small steps of the routine themselves
Stay flexible on special days and return to the pattern soon
